verses.1: Then the LORD answered Job from the whirlwind, and said:
verses.2: Who is this who darkens counsel by words without knowledge?
verses.3: Gird up your loins like a man; I will question you, and you shall make it known to me.
verses.4: Where were you when I set the earth’s foundation? Tell me, if you have understanding.
verses.5: Who set its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched the line over it?
verses.6: On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its corner stone,
verses.7: when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy?
verses.8: And who restrained the sea with doors, when it burst forth from the womb?
verses.9: When I clothed it with clouds, and thick darkness as a swaddling band,
verses.10: and fixed its limits with a barrier and doors,
verses.11: and said, “Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here your proud waves shall be stayed”?
verses.12: Have you commanded the dawn from its birth, and caused the morning to know its place?
verses.13: To take hold of the corners of the earth, and shake the wicked out of it?
verses.14: It turns like clay for the seal, and all its features are like a garment.
verses.15: The light is withheld from the wicked, and the arm that is raised is broken.
verses.16: Have you come to the springs of the sea, or walked in the recesses of the deep?
verses.17: Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?
verses.18: Have you observed the breadth of the earth? Declare, if you know all these.
verses.19: Where is the way to the dwelling of light, and where is the place of darkness?
verses.20: Can you bring them to their boundary, or do you know the paths to their house?
verses.21: Do you know, for then you would have been born, and your days would be many.
verses.22: Have you come to the treasures of snow or to the storehouses of hail, which I have reserved against the day of distress, against the day of battle and war?
verses.23: By what way is the light divided, or how does the east wind spread over the land?
verses.24: Who has carved a channel for the torrents of rain, and a way for the thunder’s voice,
verses.25: to pour out rain on a land where no one dwells, on a desert without a man in it,
verses.26: to water the wasteland, and cause the sprout of the meadow to grow?
verses.27: Who is the father of the rain, or who has begotten the dewdrops?
verses.28: From whose womb has the ice come forth? And who has given birth to the frost of the heavens?
verses.29: The waters become hidden like stone, and the face of the deep is bound fast.
verses.30: Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades, or loose the cords of Orion?
verses.31: Can you bring forth the constellations in their season, or guide the Bear and her cubs?
verses.32: Do you know the laws of the heavens, or can you set their dominion over the earth?
verses.33: Can you send your voice to the clouds, or cause the waters to flow over you?
verses.34: Can you send forth lightnings, that they may say to you, “Here we are”?
verses.35: Who has put wisdom in the heart of the one who understands, or given insight to the one who knows how to weave?
verses.36: Who can number the clouds by wisdom, or pour out the heavens’ vastness like a canopy?
verses.37: Can you, in your wisdom, direct the wings of the sky, or cause the stars to lie still?
verses.38: Can you bind the spring of the dust, or fasten the trembling sands together?
verses.39: Have you taken the lion by the claw, and filled its dens with prey?
verses.40: For they lie in wait in their dens, and remain in their lairs at dusk.
verses.41: Who provides food for the raven, when its young cry out to God, and wander for lack of food?

notes:
Notes
- v. 30: "Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades" — the Hebrew "ma'adanoth" is typically understood as "chains," but could also be metaphorical for their fixed position.
- v. 31: "the Bear and her cubs" — the Hebrew "ayish" is usually rendered as "Orion" or "constellation," but the context of a mother and cubs suggests a reference to Ursa Major.
- v. 36: "the heavens’ vastness like a canopy" — the Hebrew "nivle shel shamayim" is translated here as "the heavens’ vastness like a canopy," capturing the poetic imagery.
